summary.summary: Leicestershire's debt keeps shrinking: it repaid £44.5m of PWLB loans in 2025/26 — including £15.3m of 6.25-7.88% loans bought back at a £3.5m premium in March 2026 — taking external debt to £130.5m, its lowest for over 20 years, against a £387.5m investment portfolio and £388m of cash. The one indicator breach is a direct result: capital financing costs as a share of net revenue exceeded target because of those premiums, which the council expects to save nearly £1m a year in future interest. What remains of the debt book is dominated by £93.5m of market loans whose lenders can propose rate rises at pre-set dates (LOBO-type), a live consideration with gilt yields at their highest this century. The council has not raised a new external loan since August 2010, is £63m under-borrowed, and earned £16.6m treasury interest against a £12m budget.

signals.headline: £44.5m of PWLB repaid in 2025/26 with no new borrowing; external debt of £130.5m at 31 March 2026 is the lowest for over 20 years, against £387.5m of investments
signals.why: A shrinking, long-dated debt book backed by cash nearly three times its size leaves negligible refinancing exposure.

signals.headline: 'Capital financing costs as a percentage of net revenue stream' indicator was exceeded in 2025/26 because of £3.5m of premiums paid to repay £15.3m of 6.25-7.88% PWLB early on 31 March 2026
signals.why: A deliberate one-off cost (effective saving rate 7.16% vs a 3.50% forecast earning rate, saving nearly £1m a year in fixed interest) rather than an underlying affordability deterioration.

signals.headline: £93.5m of the remaining £130.5m debt book is market loans carrying lender options to raise the rate at pre-set dates (avg 4.41%, 37-year average life); call dates not disclosed
signals.why: With gilt yields at 20+ year highs lender options become more attractive to exercise, though the council could repay from £388m of cash if called.

compliance.notes: Strong, professionally advised (MUFG) county-council TMSS: prudential indicators, a charted four-component liability benchmark used as a live tool, an annuity MRP policy with voluntary MRP disclosed, a well-explained under-borrowing/internal-borrowing strategy, and a ratings-plus-CDS creditworthiness policy with a detailed counterparty/country/group limit matrix - every applicable core requirement scores >=2. The commercial dimension (IiLP, ~£260m held primarily for return) is well framed on no-borrowing-for-yield, PWLB access and annual exit review, but the harder commercial disclosures are deferred to the separate IiLP/Capital Strategy. Weakest areas are commercial risk disclosure in the TMSS itself (guarantees/contingent liabilities absent, statutory fair-value/contingency and formal commercial limits only partial), the absence of a quantitative portfolio risk indicator, and reporting-side omissions (no audit-qualification flag, no financial-instruments accounting disclosures, no explicit sterling-only borrowing or derivatives policy).

news_drafts.headline: Leicestershire Council's commercial income falls short while capital spending rises
news_drafts.lead: Leicestershire Council's draft accounts for 2025/26 were published on time, and its 2024/25 statements received an unmodified audit opinion — meaning auditors consider them to give a true and fair view. However, material financial pressures are evident. Net income from commercial activities has fallen to 1.0 per cent of day-to-day spending, down from the 1.3 per cent the council originally forecast. This represents a material shortfall in a revenue source the authority had been counting on. Capital spending (money spent on long-lived assets like buildings) has simultaneously risen to £181m from a forecast £164m in the first quarter of 2026-27. The council's actual external debt stands at £87m, significantly below the originally forecast £145m.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Prudential and Treasury Indicators 2026-27

news_drafts.headline: Leicestershire clears audit but economic slowdown and weak commercial income test finances
news_drafts.lead: The county council's accounts cleared audit, with debt falling to £87 million, well below a forecast of £145 million. Capital spending rose to £181 million to invest in schools, roads and buildings. Commercial income, however, fell to 1.0 per cent of net revenue spending from a forecast of 1.3 per cent. The economy contracted in April for the first time since August 2025, government borrowing rose to 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product against a March forecast of 3.6 per cent, and public sector pay accelerated to 5.1 per cent year-on-year, faster than the Bank of England's 3.25 per cent inflation target.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Prudential and Treasury Indicators 2026-27

news_drafts.headline: Leicestershire borrows £58m less than planned while ramping up capital spending
news_drafts.lead: Leicestershire County Council's actual debt stands at £87m as of September 2026, £58m below the £145m it originally forecast for the year. The undershoot occurred despite the council increasing its capital programme — money spent on long-lived assets such as buildings and equipment — to £181m from an originally planned £164m. The larger capital plan suggests the council is using internal reserves or alternative funding sources to finance investment rather than taking loans from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils. The council's 2024/25 accounts received an unmodified audit opinion, meaning the external auditor confirmed they give a true and fair view of the council's finances.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Prudential and Treasury Indicators 2026-27

findings.headline: Pooled property fund investments are now valued below invested capital, showing unrealised losses of approximately £1.4m.
findings.detail: Two UK commercial pooled property funds committed between 2015 and 2019 (Threadneedle and DTZ managed active value) now have NAV of £7.6m against capital invested of £9m. Council attributes below-cost valuations to higher interest rates and changed property market conditions compared to very low rate environment when originally invested. Threadneedle (open-ended) can be held indefinitely; DTZ (closed-ended) is returning capital as properties are sold.
findings.matters: Demonstrates value destruction in strategic property investments from interest rate and market movements; shows impact of higher rate environment on fixed-asset valuations.
findings.figures: £9m capital invested; £7.6m current NAV; ~£1.4m unrealised loss; 2.2% IRR since inception
findings.quote: Both pooled property funds have current valuations below the invested capital. This is generally due to the higher value of property when these investments were originally made (during a very low UK interest rate period) compared to the valuations in a higher UK interest rate environment.

findings.headline: Council is £102m underborrowed against Capital Financing Requirement, managing position through £335m investment balances.
findings.detail: With external debt of £87m against estimated CFR of £189m, council has substantial underborrowing position. Rather than accessing external borrowing markets, manages longer-term cash through investment balances of £335m. This demonstrates strong liquidity and financial capacity but indicates council has not needed to access markets recently and may have over-accumulated cash reserves.
findings.matters: Underborrowed position and reliance on internal investment reserves indicate strong balance sheet and borrowing capacity; relevant to understanding council's future refinancing needs and market access profile.
findings.figures: £87m external debt; £189m estimated CFR; £102m underborrowed; £335m investment balances
findings.quote: Comparing the actual external debt to the CFR, the Council is forecast to be £102m underborrowed at year end. With investment balances of £335m, this position can be managed using internal investment balances rather than more expensive external borrowing.

findings.headline: Financing costs exceeded prudential indicator by 0.1% due to premiums paid on early debt repayment.
findings.detail: Council exceeded prudential indicator for actual financing costs as percentage of net revenue stream by 0.1%, directly attributable to £8.2m premiums paid on early PWLB repayments. Council states this was exception to normal prudential adherence, driven by deliberate debt repayment strategy. Excess is immaterial but represents trade-off between prudential compliance and debt reduction objective.
findings.matters: Shows council chose to exceed its own prudential limits in pursuit of debt reduction strategy; indicates financial costs of early repayment were higher than originally budgeted.
findings.figures: 0.1% excess on financing costs as percentage of net revenue stream; £8.2m premiums paid on early repayments
findings.quote: The Council has operated within the treasury and prudential indicators... except for the actual financing costs as a % of net revenue stream by 0.1% due to the premiums payable on the early repayment of debt.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast for 2026-27 increased by £17m to £181m after MTFS approval, driven by additional government grants and rephasing.
findings.detail: Original prudential indicator set at £164m; forecast now £181m due to additional government capital grants announced after February 2026 MTFS approval and rephasing of expenditure from 2025/26 outturn. Council confirms the increase is fully funded and represents post-approval change to capital strategy, signalling either improved funding availability or rescheduling of investment schemes.
findings.matters: Material increase in capital expenditure signals either improved funding availability or rephasing of investment schemes, with implications for borrowing requirements and the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.quote: The latest estimate of capital expenditure in 2026/27 is £181m compared with the original prudential indicator of £164m. The increase is due to additional government capital grants, announced after the MTFS was approved, and the rephasing of capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Two LOBO loans totalling £20m were called by FMS and Dexia with lender options to increase rates; council repaid at par without premiums.
findings.detail: FMS loan of £10m at 4.75% coupon (maturity 2054) and Dexia loan of £10m at 4.50% coupon (maturity 2065) were subject to lender call options exercised to increase rates to significantly higher levels. Council chose to repay at par with no redemption premiums rather than accept the higher rates. This eliminates long-dated, high-legacy-cost liabilities and represents a lender-initiated refinancing and liquidity event.
findings.matters: Lender exercise of LOBO call options is a refinancing and liquidity event that extinguishes exposure to significantly higher rates on legacy loans and removes interest rate risk.
findings.figures: FMS: £10m at 4.75%, maturity 2054; Dexia: £10m at 4.50%, maturity 2065; zero premiums on LOBO repayments
findings.quote: The lender exercised their call option to change the interest rates on the loans (to a significantly higher rate). As a result, the Council took the opportunity to repay these loans, no premiums apply in these circumstances.
